title: The two Dals
hookLine: the Khalsa organized into the elders' army and the young army

lines: A NAME AND A JOB FOR EACH.
cards: Here is a tension that turns up in families, in teams, in congregations. The young want to move. The old want to keep.
The young say: you're too careful. The old say: you're too quick. Sometimes one side wins and the other drifts away.
The Khalsa, in its hard years, had both kinds of Sikh in its ranks, with real lives at stake. And tradition says that under Nawab Kapur Singh each was given a name and a job.

teach.b: Dal means a host, an army, a body of people moving together.
Tradition says that under Nawab Kapur Singh the Khalsa was organized into two of them: the Budha Dal, the army of the elders, and the Taruna Dal, the army of the young. Each had its own work.
The tellings say the Budha Dal, the older Sikhs, looked after the holy places and the steady life of the community, and gave counsel.
The Taruna Dal, the younger riders, took on the fast, dangerous work of defense, moving where they were needed. Neither was the junior partner.
The elders were not pushed aside as too slow; the young were not held back as too reckless.
In the tellings, they were separate, but not apart.

Tradition says that when the Khalsa gathered at Amritsar, both Dals came together, sat in the same sangat, and made decisions as one. The young had the elders' memory. The elders had the young's strength.

And over both stood a shared allegiance: not to a Dal, but to the Guru's way. Tradition says the Taruna Dal later grew and was divided into smaller bands, and those bands, in time, became the seeds of something bigger.
But today the point is simpler. A community needs its grandparents and its teenagers, the ones who remember why and the ones who can still run. The two Dals are a picture of how not to waste either.

how: Sikhs remember the Budha Dal and Taruna Dal as the Khalsa's organization under Nawab Kapur Singh, and Nihang Sikh groups today still carry the name Budha Dal.

o: the young riders who took on fast defense work
the whole Khalsa gathered at Amritsar as one
the elders' army, keeping holy places and counsel

games.q: two armies, one sangat — tap the pairs.

s: the elders' Dal was pushed aside as too slow
the Budha Dal cared for the holy places and gave counsel; neither Dal was the junior partner.
both Dals gathered together in one sangat at Amritsar
separate in their work, they made decisions as one.
the Taruna Dal guarded the holy places
the tellings give that to the Budha Dal; the young riders took on fast defense.

games.q: you're Nawab Kapur Singh. the young riders and the elders pull in different directions. what do you do?
o: put the young in charge; speed wins.
give each its own name and work, and gather them in one sangat.
games.why: tradition says he organized the Budha Dal and the Taruna Dal, each with its own work, meeting together at Amritsar.

practice: Bring to mind one person a good deal older than you, and let one thing they know, that you don't, come to mind. Then bring to mind someone a good deal younger, and one thing they can do that you can't anymore, or never could.
Hold the two of them side by side for a while, and if you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Budha Dal. The army of the elders, paired with the Taruna Dal, the army of the young: two bodies of the Khalsa with different work and one shared sangat.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: dal, a host or army; Budha Dal, the elders, and Taruna Dal, the young.

carryVoice: Your line: old and young together. Memory and strength, in one sangat. That's day eight hundred fifty-three.
